unit.title: Performance and optimization deep dives
unit.summary: Investigate launch, rendering, memory, networking, energy, build time, and algorithms through controlled experiments, explicit ownership, and reviewable regression evidence.

lessons.title: Measurement contracts: Instruments, signposts, and trustworthy distributions
lessons.summary: Specify the operation, environment, denominator, and uncertainty before interpreting a trace or a percentile.
objectives: Define reproducible elapsed-time, CPU, memory, and responsiveness contracts.
Pair signposts correctly through completion and failure.
Select Instruments views from a falsifiable hypothesis.
Calculate and report percentiles without hiding sample size or device conditions.

sections.title: Start with the user operation and its denominator
sections.html:
You already know an Android trace can show a smooth main thread while an API request keeps the screen waiting. The first iOS skill is equally conceptual: define what the user is waiting for. Session 023 introduced this habit; now turn it into a written contract. For a synthetic search, the beginning might be the accepted tap after validation. The end might be a rendered list that responds to a second tap. Request completion, model assignment, view appearance, and actual presentation are different ends. Pick one primary boundary and record subordinate boundaries separately.

Write the fixture, number of rows, authentication state, route, connectivity, image state, and expected output. State the unit: milliseconds per accepted search, allocated bytes per mapping, or hitch duration per second of animation. A total across twenty operations cannot be compared with a per-operation average without conversion. Also name exclusions: canceled searches, failures, retries, and timeouts. Excluding every slow failed request can manufacture an attractive success-only distribution. Keep failure rate beside success latency.

A useful contract includes a falsifier. If you suspect synchronous mapping, high elapsed latency with little mapping CPU weakens that explanation. This discipline is familiar from Perfetto, but Instruments categories and Apple presentation boundaries require their own interpretation. The goal is a repeatable question, not an impressive trace screenshot.

sections.title: Control the environment before controlling the code
sections.html:
Record device model, OS build, app revision, Xcode/compiler version, optimization configuration, installation history, and profiler attachment. Use a representative physical device for product performance claims. A simulator is a useful functional and repeatability tool, but its CPU, storage, memory pressure, rendering, and energy behavior depend on the Mac and other host workloads. A fast simulator does not certify an older supported phone. Simulator regressions can still be useful when compared on the same controlled runner.

Do not call all repeated operations warm. Distinguish a running process, previously populated application caches, OS file caches, network connection reuse, and database initialization. State how each condition is prepared. Deleting the app changes persistent fixtures and onboarding; force-quitting ends the process but does not flush every OS cache. A first iteration discarded as warm-up is a deliberate policy, not permission to discard arbitrary slow iterations later.

Thermal state, Low Power Mode, charging, background activity, and display behavior can affect results. Record them and choose a stable testing protocol; do not assume plugging in a device eliminates thermal drift. Alternate baseline and candidate runs, or randomize their order in matched batches. Keep diagnostic runs with heavy tracing separate from confirmation runs with minimal instrumentation, because the profiler itself has a cost.

sections.title: Choose evidence that can answer the hypothesis
sections.html:
Time Profiler samples executing stacks. Restrict its timeline to the signposted operation before examining a call tree; otherwise unrelated startup or idle work may dominate the display. Separate self cost from inclusive cost: an orchestration method may appear large because its descendants are expensive. Inverting the call tree can reveal shared hot leaves, while grouping by thread can separate main-thread work from worker work. A sample is neither an exact invocation count nor proof that every call takes that duration.

When elapsed time is high but sampled CPU is low, inspect waiting: task suspension, synchronous locks, file reads, network transactions, and queue dependencies. A semaphore wait on the main thread can block the UI while contributing little active CPU. A process-wide CPU chart also cannot identify which user operation caused it. Correlate the interval, thread or task, and relevant resource track.

For scrolling, use available animation/hitch and responsiveness instruments. For retention, compare Allocations generations with a Memory Graph investigation. For transfers, use network metrics and Instruments networking tools where available. Template names and capabilities vary by installed Xcode. Learn the question each view answers rather than memorizing a screenshot from a different tool release. Preserve symbol information and the matching binary so stack attribution remains reviewable.

sections.title: A paired interval is an ownership contract
sections.html:
A signpost marks application meaning on a system timeline. The example requires the Apple os module and iOS 15 or macOS 12 onward; it belongs in an Apple-platform scratch target. The checkout's Honeycomb tracer is separate instrumentation. Its existence does not imply this signpost already exists, or that local Instruments and exported telemetry have identical sampling.

import os

@available(iOS 15.0, macOS 12.0, *)
func measuredMapping(_ input: [String]) -> [String] {
    let poster = OSSignposter(
        subsystem: "example.course", category: "Mapping"
    )
    let state = poster.beginInterval(
        "MapRows", id: poster.makeSignpostID()
    )
    defer { poster.endInterval("MapRows", state) }
    return input.map { $0.uppercased() }
}

_ removes the external argument label. let binds a value without later reassignment. state identifies this interval; two overlapping calls need distinct identities even though both use the same bounded name. defer ends it when the function exits. $0 is the map closure's current string. This operation intentionally changes case; it is a syntax example, not a search-normalization recommendation.

For async work, begin before the actual operation and end after its awaited outcome, including thrown failure and cancellation. Ending immediately after constructing a Task measures scheduling instead. Names and metadata must remain bounded and approved: no patient names, tokens, or raw queries. Define whether a canceled interval is counted as latency, canceled work, or both.

sections.title: Median and p95 answer different questions
sections.html:
The median describes a central sample; p95 describes an upper-tail threshold under a stated estimator. Declare the estimator so two engineers can reproduce it. For nearest rank, sort n samples and select rank ceil(0.95 * n), counting ranks from one. Swift arrays count indexes from zero, so the corresponding index is rank minus one. With twenty samples p95 is the nineteenth value; with five samples it is the maximum. Neither makes a small experiment a reliable estimate of the population tail.

Retain raw samples, sample count, median, p95, minimum, maximum, units, and preparation conditions. Tens of runs can reveal an obvious regression, but stable tail claims generally need a larger, repeatable sample and uncertainty analysis. Confidence intervals require an appropriate statistical method and assumptions; do not invent precision by printing many decimal places. Correlated samples taken while a device heats up are not independent observations merely because there are many of them.

Do not average p95 values from two devices and call that the fleet p95. Keep cohorts separate, or combine raw observations with an explicit weighting model. Likewise, p95 of end-to-end latency is not generally the sum of each phase's p95. Different operations may be slow in different phases. Record paired phase measurements if you want to explain which phase produced the observed tail.

sections.title: Make the benchmark resistant to accidental shortcuts
sections.html:
Separate correctness checks from the measured interval, but make the result observable. An optimized compiler can remove useless pure work when no result matters. A benchmark that repeatedly overwrites an unused local may test less than its author expects. Store a result that the harness inspects after measurement, validate its contract, and keep the same harness for both versions. Avoid adding expensive assertions or logging inside only one measured implementation.

Place fixture construction outside the block for a mapping-only question. If fixture loading belongs to the product operation, measure that larger boundary too. Reset mutable state between iterations according to the declared cache policy. A candidate that memoizes the fixture after its first run and a baseline that recomputes it answer different questions unless reuse is the proposed product behavior. Also inspect whether asynchronous work has actually finished before the measurement ends.

XCTest clock, CPU, memory, launch, and signpost metrics measure different things. Set iteration options deliberately and inspect the runner's recorded output rather than equating a loop count with retained observations. Performance baselines on a noisy shared simulator need variance-aware interpretation. A test that times out or produces incorrect output is a failed experiment, not a slow sample to quietly omit. Report instrumentation overhead and any missing artifact explicitly.

sections.title: Read existing instrumentation without claiming a profile
sections.html:
The verified Performance namespace points to a shared tracer, and its search extension creates a small set of context tags. Follow a caller to learn where a span starts, which operation ends it, and whether asynchronous completion is included. Source presence proves an instrumentation path exists; it does not prove the path ran, the exporter accepted it, or the dashboard's aggregation matches your contract. Reading these files is an audit, not profiling.

A trace report should connect evidence to a decision: the selected interval contains a hot synchronous mapping stack; a candidate reduces that work while preserving output; screen-level confirmation remains required. State what would overturn that conclusion. A tall flame graph without fixture and configuration leaves another engineer unable to reproduce your reasoning. A single percentage with no raw samples hides even more.

Android analogies remain useful for method: trace sections resemble signposts, and benchmark fixtures resemble controlled microbenchmarks. They stop at runtime semantics, tooling attribution, startup definitions, and platform memory limits. Keep a checklist of those boundaries as you learn. By the end of this lesson, your strongest artifact is a reproducible experiment specification with blank measurement cells until you actually run it, rather than a premature assertion that the app is fast.

quiz.question: What does nearest-rank p95 mean for five recorded samples?
options: The average of the slowest two values.
The largest sample, with substantial uncertainty about the population tail.
A reliable production service-level guarantee.
quiz.explanation: ceil(0.95 × 5) is rank five. The arithmetic is exact, but five observations provide weak tail evidence; state the estimator and sample size.

quiz.question: A signposted operation has long elapsed time and little sampled CPU. What should you inspect next?
options: Waiting, resource transactions, and scheduling within that interval.
Every class allocation across the app's entire lifetime.
Only the function with the most samples in an unrelated interval.
quiz.explanation: Elapsed time includes waits. Correlate the operation with task, thread, network, and I/O evidence before choosing a CPU optimization.

quiz.question: A Task starts inside an interval, but the interval ends before its work finishes. What was measured?
options: The full user operation automatically.
A device-independent latency.
Creation or scheduling up to the interval end, not the awaited outcome.
quiz.explanation: An interval only covers its actual lifetime. Pair the end with completion, error, or cancellation under an explicit ownership rule.

exercise.brief: Design a controlled mapping benchmark and a separate search-to-usable-results experiment. Implement percentile arithmetic with synthetic samples, without calling them device observations.
steps: Write operation, fixture, environment, cache policy, and failure denominator before running anything.
Implement a nearest-rank percentile helper and test empty, one-element, and twenty-element input.
Draw one mapping interval inside the longer UI operation, including failure and cancellation ends.
Prepare a report template with raw samples, sample count, median, p95, range, conditions, and unresolved device questions.
acceptance: Nearest-rank p95 of integers 1 through 20 is 19; this is arithmetic evidence only.
Empty input returns absence and invalid percentile requests have a stated precondition.
Every before/after comparison uses the same fixture and declared reset policy.
Physical-device confirmation and measurement status are explicit; blank observations are never replaced with invented timings.
exercise.solution:
This standalone helper operates on finite nonnegative samples, such as elapsed milliseconds. It is not a statistical confidence calculation. Validate the input contract at the harness boundary and retain originals before sorting.

func nearestRank(_ samples: [Double], percentile p: Double) -> Double? {
    precondition(p > 0 && p <= 1)
    precondition(samples.allSatisfy { $0.isFinite && $0 >= 0 })
    guard !samples.isEmpty else { return nil }
    let ordered = samples.sorted()
    let rank = Int((p * Double(ordered.count)).rounded(.up))
    return ordered[max(1, rank) - 1]
}

The external second label is percentile:, while p is the internal name. Double? permits absence for an empty dataset. guard exits early. Rounding upward implements the rank definition, and subtracting one converts it to an array index. For (1...20).map(Double.init), p95 is nineteen. Do not use this helper's p50 as an interpolated even-sample median without explaining the distinction: nearest-rank p50 selects the tenth of twenty values, while a conventional sample median averages the tenth and eleventh.

The worked report has columns for revision, physical device, OS, configuration, fixture, reset policy, sample index, outcome, total milliseconds, mapping milliseconds, and thermal notes. Leave timing fields unmeasured. State: “Mapping will be diagnosed with a signpost and Time Profiler; responsiveness will be confirmed with an actual interaction on the target phone.” Baseline/candidate order alternates by batch, and all errors remain counted separately. Attach raw records and matching trace/result artifacts after execution. This separates a tested arithmetic helper from a still-pending performance claim.

repo.label: Shared app tracer
repo.why: Verified tracer entry point; source inspection does not establish runtime samples or a measured improvement.

repo.label: Bounded search context
repo.why: Existing context tag construction provides actual instrumentation vocabulary to inspect before proposing new intervals.

checklist: I can state begin/end events, units, exclusions, and sample count.
I can separate simulator diagnosis from device confirmation.
I can explain inclusive samples, elapsed waiting, and instrumentation overhead.
I can reproduce percentile arithmetic and state uncertainty.

lessons.title: Launch and binary size: the path to a first usable screen
lessons.summary: Separate process startup, first presentation, deferred work, resume, and download size while preserving routing and account correctness.
objectives: Define cold launch, warm launch, and resume experiments explicitly.
Trace the critical path from process preparation to usable content.
Classify startup work by necessity and dependency without hiding later stalls.
Measure binary, resource, download, and installed sizes as different quantities.

sections.title: Cold, warm, and resume are experimental states
sections.html:
An Android engineer distinguishes cold process creation from returning to a live Activity. Bring that instinct to iOS, but avoid treating the labels as identical platform definitions. A process launch starts an application process. A resume returns an existing application to foreground activity and may still need expensive restoration or refresh. Cold and warm launches differ in system preparation and cached resources, not simply in whether your own dictionary has values. Apple describes cold launches after reboot or a long period without launch, and warm launches with helpful system state already resident.

Write how you establish each condition. A terminated-process launch after one previous launch is a repeatable laboratory category; it does not prove all system caches are cold. Reinstalling changes app data and often creates onboarding work. Rebooting changes broader state, so record settling time and unavoidable system variability. Separate first install, ordinary signed-out launch, returning-account launch, and deep-link launch instead of blending them into one favorable median.

Warm launch should never mean “press Home and immediately reopen” without checking whether the process survived. That may be a resume. Likewise, a cache hit does not define the operating system's launch category. Preserve both dimensions in your report: process state and application data state. This prevents an optimization of an in-memory cache from being advertised as a cold-start improvement.

sections.title: Draw the startup dependency path
sections.html:
Launch contains work before your first familiar delegate callback: loading code and dependencies, runtime preparation, and initializers. The dynamic loader, commonly called dyld, resolves and prepares loaded images. Framework count, executable layout, and initialization can matter, but their actual cost depends on platform and build. Avoid assigning a universal millisecond penalty per framework. Inspect a launch trace and the archived product before selecting a link strategy.

After process preparation come application setup, root presentation, layout, and the first committed and presented frame. The user may still see a spinner. Define a second endpoint for usable content: the correct route is visible, blocking initialization has finished, and a meaningful interaction succeeds. A signpost ending when a root controller is assigned cannot independently certify screen presentation. Even viewDidAppear is a lifecycle callback rather than a pixel-level measurement of every ready state.

Draw dependencies as work that must precede other work. If account reconciliation determines which route is legal, routing depends on reconciliation. Analytics configuration may be independent, but some instrumentation must start early to observe launch. The critical path is the longest necessary dependency chain, not the sum of every concurrent phase. Increasing parallelism on noncritical branches can add contention without shortening the path. Include first interaction after presentation so deferred work cannot quietly reintroduce the delay.

sections.title: Audit what this checkout actually does
sections.html:
The verified delegate callback contains a startup subspan, makes the window key and visible, then calls app.initApp and the application lifecycle layer. defer ends that callback's subspan; it does not mean every promise, task, or eventual screen update finishes before the span ends. Follow the parent startup span and later completion paths when defining the measurement. The source gives you likely boundaries and dependencies, not recorded launch time.

The application initializer creates a loading view, observes its animation through a promise, monitors reachability, removes cached URL responses, and calls migration logic. These are concrete audit subjects. Do not remove cache clearing just because it might add I/O; first establish its correctness and freshness purpose. Do not defer migration past a consumer that requires the new schema. The comment about reconciling partial account and credential state deserves particular attention because changing order could alter authentication behavior.

The launch router is an adapter toward a future scene cutover according to its own documentation. Do not describe that cutover as complete. UI lifecycle modernization and performance optimization are different changes. Read the active app route and manifests rather than assuming every modern UIKit example matches this checkout. Your exercise remains a scratch design: no initialization, migration, or routing behavior is changed in the client.

sections.title: Deferring work requires a correctness and lifetime plan
sections.html:
Classify each startup operation as required before first presentation, required before usable content, opportunistic later work, or unnecessary under the current route. For each, document dependencies, ownership, failure handling, and cancellation. A blank root frame that arrives sooner while blocking the first tap is not the intended outcome. A useful signed-out shell may be valid before public data arrives; an account-sensitive screen must not show old-account content during reconciliation.

Lazy initialization exchanges upfront cost for first-use cost. Inspect whether the first scroll, search tap, or keyboard appearance now pays the delay. Batch later work and give it an explicit owner; creating many unstructured tasks can extend launch CPU contention and retain services indefinitely. Task {} inside MainActor code may inherit that isolation. It is not a magic “after launch on a background thread” command. Session 016's compiler and isolation caveats still apply.

Do not block the main thread waiting for asynchronous initialization with semaphores or synchronous promise waits. Design a state machine that represents loading, ready, and failure, then commit the legal next state. The analogy to Android startup initializers helps with dependency order, but iOS launch termination behavior, delegate/scene callbacks, and API availability have different rules. Security initialization and data migrations need owners and recoverable failure paths before performance tradeoffs are approved.

sections.title: Measure first frame and usability separately
sections.html:
Use the launch instrument available in your installed Instruments to identify preparation, main-thread work, and presentation delays. For repeatable automation, XCTest offers XCTApplicationLaunchMetric. Current Apple documentation directs users from the older application-launch signpost metric to this metric. Its default initializer can include extended launch tasks; waitUntilResponsive: is a separate initializer choice. Confirm the exact available API and recorded boundary in your SDK rather than inheriting old lesson syntax unquestioned.

import XCTest

final class ScratchLaunchTests: XCTestCase {
    @MainActor
    func testLaunch() {
        let app = XCUIApplication()
        let options = XCTMeasureOptions()
        options.iterationCount = 10
        measure(metrics: [XCTApplicationLaunchMetric()], options: options) {
            app.launch()
        }
    }
}

This is an iOS UI-test-target example, not standalone Swift and not a client test already run. app is an automation proxy. iterationCount configures the harness; inspect the result bundle for actual retained measurements. The method is MainActor-isolated because UI automation APIs carry that isolation in modern SDKs. Ten requested iterations demonstrate syntax, not statistically strong p95 evidence. Document termination, fixture reset, and runner launch behavior. Add a separate readiness assertion and operation measurement for synthetic usable content; do not assume XCTest's idleness heuristic equals your product's readiness contract.

Compare representative devices in separate cohorts. Retain failures, raw samples, and tool versions. A profiler run identifies a cause; equivalent unprofiled runs check whether the diagnosed change affects the intended endpoint.

sections.title: Binary size has several different denominators
sections.html:
Distinguish executable bytes, embedded frameworks, resources, compressed download, installed app footprint, and runtime memory. An archive can contain symbols and multiple artifacts that are not the user's download. App thinning and compression affect distributed size. A raw archive directory comparison is not a valid claim about installed bytes on a particular device. Retain the export method, architecture, configuration, asset treatment, and size report with your comparison.

Inspect a link map or supported size-analysis output to attribute growth to code and dependencies. Removing an unused dependency may shrink the dependency graph, but code stripping, Objective-C metadata, linker flags, and resources influence the final result. Static linking can allow useful elimination and optimization; it can also duplicate code across independently linked products. Dynamic frameworks affect loading and sharing differently. Do not declare either universally smaller or faster.

The checked-in Tuist app manifest specifies -Osize for an App Clip release configuration. That is a source setting, not proof of the effective legacy build setting or current App Store policy. Do not teach the size-limit number in its comment as a timeless requirement. Measure the generated target and archived artifact used by the actual release route. The manifest migration means legacy SPM/Xcode and Tuist settings must be distinguished whenever you infer product behavior.

sections.title: Reduce bytes and work without deleting the contract
sections.html:
Assets are often a separate opportunity from Swift code. Audit duplicate images, unnecessary resolution, localized resources, and product-specific bundles. An image used by a supported variant is not unused just because the primary app's visible route did not display it. Preserve accessibility, localization, offline error states, and supported device quality. Resource pruning should start with ownership and consumers, not a search for large files followed by deletion.

Compiler options also create tradeoffs. -Osize favors code size, while other optimization modes make different choices; neither guarantees the fastest launch. Whole-module optimization can improve runtime optimization and alter compilation cost. Inlining can reduce call overhead while increasing binary size. Changes to public module boundaries or link flags require functional and configuration coverage, especially with Objective-C registration. Keep these as reviewable hypotheses until the appropriate artifact and device measurements exist.

Finish a launch report with first frame, usable content, first interaction, size dimensions, correctness scenarios, and unresolved limitations. Show returning account, signed-out, deep-link, migration, and offline paths as separate fixtures where relevant. A launch improvement that breaks a deep link or displays another account's data fails the experiment. Session 042 will combine these boundaries into a lab and regression gate; here you are learning to make startup work and size decisions auditable.

quiz.question: Does force-quitting and reopening prove a cold launch with all caches empty?
options: Yes, every cache belongs to the app process.
No, process termination and system or disk cache state are distinct.
Yes, if the opening screen is a spinner.
quiz.explanation: Force-quitting changes process state. It does not flush every system cache or erase persisted data; record the specific experiment category.

quiz.question: A deferred initializer blocks the first search tap. How should the result be assessed?
options: First-frame time alone proves success.
Deferred work never affects user performance.
Measure first interaction and usability alongside first frame.
quiz.explanation: Deferral can move cost to the next operation. The full contract includes a usable screen and an interaction, with initialization dependencies preserved.

quiz.question: Which comparison supports a device download-size claim?
options: Equivalent exported/thinned reports with the same distribution method and device conditions.
Uncompressed archive folder size versus a simulator executable.
The number of imports in AppDelegate.
quiz.explanation: Archive, executable, installed, and compressed download sizes have different denominators. Compare the artifact that represents the intended distribution.

exercise.brief: Create a startup dependency audit for the active delegate/application paths and a proposed synthetic launch experiment; do not alter client initialization.
steps: Trace callback subspans, window presentation, loading view, migration, and routing readiness from the source anchors.
Classify five operations by the earliest safe phase and record dependencies.
Specify signed-out, returning-account, and deep-link fixtures plus terminated-process and resume conditions.
Write separate first-frame, usable-content, first-interaction, and exported-size evidence fields.
acceptance: The audit distinguishes callback completion from completion of asynchronous startup.
Migration and account reconciliation remain dependencies of consumers that need them.
Cold/warm labels have an explicit preparation procedure and uncertain OS cache state is acknowledged.
No timing, size saving, scene migration, or release-policy claim is fabricated.
exercise.solution:
A worked dependency audit places appearance restoration before bar construction because the delegate source states that bars snapshot appearance. It places account reconciliation before presenting an authenticated route, and schema migration before accessing a consumer requiring the migrated store. It puts a potentially deferrable telemetry operation in an unresolved category until its dependency and instrumentation needs are understood. The window callback and loading-view promise are separate boundaries.

The experiment sheet records revision, effective configuration, phone/OS, installation history, route fixture, process preparation, cache policy, and thermal condition. Row one is a terminated-process signed-out launch after a previous successful run. Row two is returning from background with process survival verified. Row three is a deep-link launch into a permitted synthetic destination. None is silently renamed “cold.” First frame comes from the supported launch metric; usable content ends at the defined readiness state and presented route; a follow-up interaction verifies that readiness has meaning.

For size, compare the same export/thinning report before and after a hypothetical dependency change, with executable, resources, frameworks, download, and installed figures separated. Leave all observations blank until execution. The recommendation is conditional: “Investigate the longest measured required startup phase; any deferral must preserve account and migration order and must pass first-interaction validation.” That is a concrete, reviewable design even before device access exists.

I can draw required startup dependencies and asynchronous endpoints.
I can measure first frame and first usable interaction separately.

lessons.title: Rendering and hitches: frame deadlines, list work, and SwiftUI invalidation
lessons.summary: Trace commit and render delays, narrow state dependencies, preserve row identity, and budget main-thread work during real interactions.
objectives: Distinguish a hang, a commit hitch, and a render hitch.
Use refresh cadence as a deadline context rather than a universal per-function allowance.
Explain body evaluation, dependency invalidation, identity, layout, and presentation separately.
Design scrolling experiments that preserve content, cancellation, accessibility, and correctness.

sections.title: A frame crosses more than your main thread
sections.html:
Think of Android input, composition or View traversal, and rendering as a pipeline with deadlines. iOS also separates event processing and UI updates in the app from rendering and presentation. UIKit and SwiftUI produce a representation that Core Animation commits; the render server and GPU perform further work before the display presents the result. This is a conceptual analogy, not a one-to-one mapping of Android RenderThread or recomposition internals.

A commit hitch occurs when application work misses its commit deadline. A render hitch occurs when rendering misses its deadline even though the app committed in time. A hang describes an interval of unresponsiveness, often around a discrete interaction; a hitch interrupts continuous motion such as scrolling or an animation. The same blocking main-thread operation can contribute to both, depending on when it happens. Fixing CPU work cannot explain every render hitch.

Select a repeatable gesture and correlate the hitch with app and render tracks. Main-thread mapping near a missed commit suggests one path; costly compositing after a timely commit suggests another. Do not diagnose by average CPU alone. A low overall average can hide one badly timed burst, and a busy worker can be harmless until it competes for resources needed by the UI. Preserve timeline context when choosing a candidate fix.

sections.title: Refresh cadence is not an allocation for each method
sections.html:
At 60 Hz, refreshes are roughly 16.7 milliseconds apart; at 120 Hz, roughly 8.3. These are useful arithmetic constraints, not a promise that every function gets that much time. Input handling, state derivation, layout, layer updates, rendering, and system overhead share pipeline deadlines. Several individually small operations can collectively miss a deadline. Dynamic refresh behavior, buffering, and scheduling also mean the entire path is not accurately modeled as one isolated stopwatch per refresh.

Report hitch duration or rate with its denominator and the interaction interval. Average frames per second can hide pauses separated by smooth periods. A shorter gesture can dilute or amplify a hitch-rate comparison, so use the same route, duration, content size, direction changes, and image/cache policy. Include a fast fling and a slower drag where each represents actual use; they expose different loading and layout behavior. Keep Dynamic Type, localization, and accessibility settings in the experiment contract.

Use a physical device for claims about smoothness and GPU behavior. The simulator's host GPU and display conditions cannot certify a phone's deadline performance. A 120 Hz-capable device may not remain at that cadence during every run. Record actual relevant conditions and avoid claiming a frame was missed merely because a function exceeded a guessed constant. The trace's deadline evidence is more informative than a hard-coded “16 ms means bad” rule.

sections.title: Keep synchronous UI work bounded
sections.html:
MainActor organizes access to UI state; it does not make expensive work cheap. A Task created in an isolated UI callback can inherit that actor. Synchronous sorting, decoding, or filesystem access inside it can still prevent the UI from processing input. An await later in the closure does not retroactively move earlier work away. Kotlin's withContext(Dispatchers.Default) is a useful reminder to choose CPU execution deliberately, but Swift isolation and executor selection follow different rules.

Prefer removing redundant work before adding concurrency. Derive rows once per accepted data revision rather than sorting them during every body evaluation. Break a large CPU operation into cancellation-aware chunks when appropriate, and return immutable Sendable snapshots to a small UI commit. Explicit worker isolation can keep computation away from MainActor, but actor methods serialize work and can become their own bottleneck. Check the effective compiler/language settings before relying on nonisolated async execution; modern defaults differ from older semantics.

Do not block a cooperative executor with a semaphore while waiting for an async child, or block MainActor on a worker that needs MainActor to finish. That is a correctness and responsiveness hazard. A dedicated queue for genuinely blocking legacy I/O needs a bounded, cancellation-aware bridge and ownership design. The unit teaches those boundaries; it does not prescribe Task.detached as a general performance remedy.

sections.title: An invalidated body is work, not a guaranteed redraw
sections.html:
A SwiftUI view is a value describing UI. Its body can be evaluated repeatedly when dependencies change. Evaluation, reconciliation, layout, layer commit, and visible presentation are different events. A print in body counts evaluations with its own overhead; it does not count displayed frames. Do not put network requests, decoder construction, or persistent writes in body. A computed property called there also runs there unless it has another explicit strategy.

With ObservableObject, object-change publication can invalidate observing views more broadly than the property-access tracking offered by the Observation framework. With @Observable on supported systems, body dependencies are based on observable properties read during evaluation. This can narrow updates, but does not promise that no parent, layout, environment, or identity change will affect the subtree. @Published and @Observable are different mechanisms, not interchangeable punctuation.

Read only relevant state near the view that uses it. Splitting a large body into leaf views helps only if dependencies and inputs become narrower. Passing the same frequently changing aggregate to every row can retain broad updates. A read hidden inside a helper can still establish a dependency. Measure body update duration and frequency with the SwiftUI tooling available in your Xcode, and correlate with hitches. Optimization means reducing relevant work while preserving the state displayed to the user.

sections.title: Small syntax details protect stable identity
sections.html:
This iOS 17+ SwiftUI example separates immutable row input from a changing progress property. It is a scratch target, not an instruction to migrate the checkout's existing view models.

import SwiftUI
import Observation

struct Row: Identifiable {
    let id: String
    let title: String
}
@MainActor @Observable
final class ScreenState {
    var rows: [Row] = []
    var progress = 0
}
@MainActor
struct ProgressLabel: View {
    let state: ScreenState
    var body: some View { Text("Loaded \(state.progress)") }
}
struct ResultRow: View {
    let row: Row
    var body: some View { Text(row.title) }
}

Identifiable requires an id with stable meaning. final prohibits subclassing; it is not the cause of observation. The macro creates observation machinery, while @MainActor states isolation. some View hides a concrete return type without storing an arbitrary view existential. String interpolation inserts progress into display text. The progress label reads progress; a ResultRow receives only a row snapshot. A parent that reads progress itself can still establish a broader dependency.

Use domain IDs in ForEach for changing collections. Generating a new UUID during each evaluation destroys stable identity. Index identity can attach state to the wrong item after insertion or reordering. Duplicate domain IDs also violate the intended identity contract. Equatable shortcuts must include every input relevant to visible content and actions; ignoring meaningful changes to reduce updates creates stale UI.

sections.title: Lazy lists still contain eager work
sections.html:
LazyVStack defers some view creation; it does not make every array transformation lazy, bound all images in memory, or eliminate layout. A filter, sorted, or Array(enumerated()) expression supplying the collection can still run before row rendering. A nested container that groups many rows may change how much work is realized together. The active search list documents a flattened-row approach and uses LazyVStack, sections, and row identities. Inspect the invoked row builder and real trace before assuming the comment proves smoothness.

UIKit reuse similarly reduces repeated view creation but does not make cell configuration free. Cancel obsolete image work, reset visible state, preserve the current item identity when an asynchronous result arrives, and avoid synchronous disk reads during binding. Diffable snapshots cost CPU and memory too; construct and apply them with framework constraints, and update only the intended revision. Prefetch is speculative work with an owner and cancellation event, not permission to load the whole dataset.

Self-sizing and repeated layout invalidation can add passes. The checked-in AutolayoutCollectionView invalidates intrinsic size when bounds and intrinsic size differ. That is an audit point, not proof of a layout loop. Measure call frequency and constraint behavior. Preserve Dynamic Type and correct content sizing; replacing self-sizing with a guessed fixed height can improve a narrow trace while clipping real text.

sections.title: Use Instruments 26 lanes as versioned diagnostic clues
sections.html:
Apple's WWDC25 guidance introduces a SwiftUI instrument in Instruments 26 with an Update Groups lane, long body/representable/other-update lanes, and detailed update tracks. Start at a hitch, select the related update interval, and correlate its work with Time Profiler. When CPU rises while Update Groups is empty, investigate other work instead of assuming SwiftUI caused the spike. Follow update causes and effects to find unnecessary sequences; a single cheap update can still be repeated excessively.

Orange/red highlights and the tool's thresholds are diagnostic classifications for that version, not universal per-frame budgets or proof that a particular update caused a hitch. Check the installed Xcode/Instruments version and device OS support before expecting these tracks. A missing lane can reflect tool/runtime capability, not absence of work. The linked current documentation describes capabilities; checkout tools-version headers, package pins, and target language settings do not establish that the instrument ran locally.

Use the evidence to distinguish slow body computation, costly UIKit representable updates, and unnecessary update chains. Preserve the selected interval and causal view with the trace. Verify that a narrowed dependency actually reduces relevant work and still updates visible state correctly.

sections.title: Compositing and image work need separate hypotheses
sections.html:
Complex masks, shadows, transparency, blur, and large layered surfaces can make rendering expensive. Their cost depends on composition, scale, clipping, cache behavior, and hardware. Avoid folklore such as “all rounded corners are slow” or enabling rasterization on every layer. Rasterization creates another cached bitmap with memory and invalidation costs; animated scale or changing content may make it counterproductive. Use render evidence and visual comparison to select a bounded change.

Image fetch completion does not necessarily mean pixel decoding is finished. A large image may defer decoding until display, causing work during scrolling; shrinking its onscreen frame does not necessarily reduce decoded memory. Session 039 develops image size and downsampling. Here separate network wait, disk read, decode, view update, layout, and rendering so one broad “image load” interval cannot conceal the cause.

For a scrolling report, attach the gesture protocol, dataset, traces with selected hitch intervals, and before/after distributions once measured. Verify selection, focus, row state, image correctness after reuse, accessibility, and cancellation on route exit. A faster list that displays stale photos fails the acceptance contract. Specialist Metal or shader analysis may be needed for a persistent render-server bottleneck; the course provides triage and experiment design rather than claiming to exhaust GPU engineering.

quiz.question: The app commits on time, but the render server misses presentation. What is the primary classification?
options: A render hitch, requiring render-side evidence.
Proof that a network request blocked the main thread.
A SwiftUI body evaluation count.
quiz.explanation: Timely application commit and late rendering indicate a render hitch. Correlate compositing/GPU evidence before changing application CPU code.

quiz.question: Does LazyVStack make an input array's sorted() call lazy?
options: Yes, it postpones all upstream code.
No, the input transformation can still be eager.
Only if every row has a UUID generated in body.
quiz.explanation: Lazy view realization does not change Array.sorted into a lazy operation. Stable identity is a separate requirement.

quiz.question: Why is a body print count insufficient as a frame count?
options: SwiftUI never evaluates body during scrolling.
Every evaluation is immediately presented.
Evaluation, reconciliation, layout, commit, and presentation are separate stages.
quiz.explanation: An evaluated description may lead to different amounts of downstream work. Use actual rendering and hitch evidence; logging can also perturb timing.

exercise.brief: Design and inspect a synthetic 500-row scrolling screen with progress updates, stable identity, and asynchronous image placeholders. Produce a dependency and hitch investigation plan.
steps: Use stable synthetic row IDs and compute any sorted/filter projection at the accepted data revision boundary.
Place progress reads in a separate leaf and explain every state read in the parent and rows.
Specify fixed gesture duration, Dynamic Type, device/display conditions, and cold/warm image conditions.
Inspect the active search list and intrinsic-size subclass as audit evidence; retain actual trace fields as pending until execution.
acceptance: Inserting at the start or reordering retains the correct state and action for each domain ID.
Progress updates do not trigger fresh network requests or expensive mapping from body.
The report distinguishes commit and render hitches and contains no invented frame improvement.
Dynamic Type, reuse image identity, route-exit cancellation, and a follow-up interaction are checked.
exercise.solution:
A worked design has a data owner that accepts a complete immutable row revision, performs the declared projection once, and exposes rows to a list. The list renders ForEach(rows) with stable IDs and passes each row to ResultRow. The progress leaf reads only progress. Keep the owner alive through an appropriate root state/lifetime mechanism; constructing a fresh observable owner during each body evaluation would reset both data and identity. No equality shortcut omits action or title changes.

For images, the row passes an item identity and requested pixel size to a bounded loader. An obsolete completion must verify identity before display; cancellation handles avoid wasted work after leaving the screen. Placeholders preserve sizing so image arrivals do not unexpectedly relayout the whole list. The design does not infer that a tiny frame causes downsampling.

The report labels “MainActor projection during gesture” and “render-server compositing during gesture” as competing hypotheses. Select a hitch interval, compare deadline tracks, then inspect the relevant stacks. Verify the same gesture without the heavy profiler after a candidate change. Keep separate measurements for cold image data and repeated scrolling. Expected evidence is a reproducible gesture, correctness results, trace intervals, sample count, and hitch denominator; all performance observations remain pending until the scratch app is actually run on a representative phone.

lessons.title: Memory: ARC, copy-on-write, autorelease, and decoded images
lessons.summary: Explain retained and transient memory, diagnose ownership, and downsample images using pixel budgets instead of compressed file size.
objectives: Separate live objects, allocation churn, transient peak, and process footprint.
Trace strong ownership cycles and task lifetime without unsafe weak-capture shortcuts.
Explain value semantics and the conditions that make copy-on-write expensive.
Calculate decoded-image estimates and implement a bounded ImageIO thumbnail example.

sections.title: Measure retained population and transient peak separately
sections.html:
Android heap analysis teaches you to ask who retains a screen. On iOS that question remains useful, but garbage collection and ARC have different lifetime mechanisms. Also, managed objects are only part of an app's footprint. Pixel buffers, mapped files, framework allocations, GPU resources, and temporary decode storage can matter. A count of Swift objects is not a complete memory budget. Decide whether you are investigating retained growth, allocation churn, or the peak during one operation.

Use a repeatable route: enter the synthetic screen, load the same fixture, leave, and settle according to the ownership contract. In Allocations, compare generations or selected intervals to identify surviving populations and repeated allocations. In Memory Graph, inspect strong paths from roots to the object that should have been released. Leaks can identify some lost allocations, but reachable objects retained by an unwanted owner may require explicit reasoning. “Leaks reports nothing” is not proof of correct lifetime.

Track both steady state and peak. A pipeline can release everything eventually yet briefly hold compressed bytes, a full decoded image, a thumbnail, and copies simultaneously. On a physical device, resource pressure may terminate the process; simulator headroom does not establish a safe budget. There is no universal per-app memory limit to transplant from Android or a particular phone. Retain device and pressure context with the evidence.

sections.title: ARC counts ownership; it does not understand your feature
sections.html:
ARC manages strong references to class instances. A strong property or closure capture can extend an instance's life; reference cycles can keep each other alive after external owners disappear. A value containing a reference does not remove this ownership. A struct view model containing a closure that captures a controller can still keep the controller alive through the closure's retained context. Draw the graph before changing captures.

weak references do not keep an object alive and become nil when it deallocates; they need optional handling. unowned expresses a stronger lifetime assumption and can trap if the referenced object is gone. Prefer a design with a clear owner instead of substituting unowned for performance. [weak self] changes capture ownership, but guard let self else { return } creates a strong binding. If that binding remains live across an await, the owner can remain retained for the operation.

A stored unstructured task that strongly captures its owning screen can create a retention cycle or extend lifetime until completion. Canceling in deinit alone may never run at the intended moment because the task is retaining the owner. Define cancellation at route exit or feature teardown, preserve cooperative checks, and avoid publishing stale results. Weak captures and cancellation solve different problems: one influences retention, the other stops owned work when it is no longer needed.

sections.title: Value semantics do not mean a deep copy on every assignment
sections.html:
Swift arrays and other standard collections use copy-on-write storage optimizations while preserving value semantics. Assigning an array gives another logical value; buffers can initially be shared. Mutating a shared value may require copying its storage. Mutating uniquely owned storage can avoid that copy. This is unlike assuming every Kotlin List assignment is an immutable independent value; Kotlin interfaces alone do not promise snapshot semantics.

var original = Array(repeating: 1, count: 10_000)
var edited = original
edited[0] = 2
// original[0] is still 1; edited[0] is 2.

Array(repeating:count:) creates the fixture. The assignment preserves independent observable values. The mutation can trigger storage separation; do not promise a particular allocation instruction because optimization and bridging can change implementation details. To study copying, make both results observable and inspect allocation evidence under the same optimized configuration.

Repeatedly storing old snapshots while mutating the newest can retain many buffers. Repeated output = output + [item] can allocate and copy growing arrays; append with sensible capacity can reduce growth work. ArraySlice can keep a large backing allocation alive for a tiny logical range. Copying a needed small slice into an array trades immediate work for releasing the large buffer. Arrays of class references copy references, not independent deep copies of the objects. COW never makes concurrently mutating the same variable safe.

sections.title: Objective-C temporary lifetime crosses Swift boundaries
sections.html:
Foundation and UIKit interoperability can involve autoreleased Objective-C objects. An autorelease pool delays release of registered temporaries until the pool drains; it is not a Swift garbage collector. UI event processing normally provides pools, but a long synchronous loop using bridged APIs can accumulate temporary objects before a normal drain. A local autoreleasepool { ... } around a bounded synchronous chunk can reduce that temporary peak when evidence identifies this source.

The Swift closure is synchronous. You cannot wrap a suspending async operation with an ordinary autorelease pool and assume its entire lifetime is covered. Async tasks may suspend and resume on different threads. Similarly, starting a callback operation inside a pool does not place its eventual callback allocations in that lexical pool. The active Objective-C image cache starts a URLSession data task inside @autoreleasepool; its completion handler runs later. Read that timing before inferring what the pool actually releases.

A pool does not free an image still retained by your result array, a view, or a cache. It does not fix a strong cycle, release a GPU surface on demand, or erase sensitive storage. Keep the returned result alive through ARC if it must escape a chunk, and release temporary intermediates as soon as ownership permits. Compare peaks before and after an isolated change. The old Apple guide supports the mechanism, but its manual-retain examples are historical context, not modern Swift implementation guidance.

sections.title: Compressed image bytes are the wrong decoded budget
sections.html:
A JPEG file can be small because it is compressed while its decoded pixels are large. A theoretical 4000 × 3000 image at four bytes per pixel needs 48,000,000 bytes, about 45.8 MiB, before other storage and overhead. This is arithmetic, not a measured allocation. Row padding, pixel format, extended range, color conversion, intermediate surfaces, and framework behavior can change the actual footprint. When available, bytesPerRow * height describes a particular decoded CGImage buffer more directly than the file's Data count.

UI dimensions are often in points. To request a sharp 80-point square on a scale-three display, plan approximately 240 pixels per side. A square four-byte-per-pixel buffer at that size is 230,400 bytes, excluding overhead. Changing UIImageView bounds to 80 points does not necessarily decode the source to 240 pixels. Scaling after full decoding may hold both the large and small images at peak. Downsampling aims to avoid needlessly materializing full-size pixels for a thumbnail.

Budget active decodes as well as retained thumbnails. Four overlapping large decodes can create a peak even with a small final cache. Bound concurrency and input dimensions; limit compressed bytes and frame counts for untrusted sources. Animated formats and multi-frame files need a separate policy. Cache costs should represent decoded storage and transformations, not only compressed download size.

sections.title: Read an ImageIO downsampler line by line
sections.html:
This synchronous Apple-platform function produces the first image as a bounded thumbnail. Use it in a deliberate bounded worker path; calling it directly from body or cell configuration still blocks that caller. Foundation and ImageIO are required.

import Foundation
import ImageIO

enum ThumbnailError: Error { case invalidSize, invalidSource, decodeFailed }

func thumbnail(at url: URL, maxPixelSize: Int) throws -> CGImage {
    guard (1...4096).contains(maxPixelSize) else {
        throw ThumbnailError.invalidSize
    }
    let sourceOptions = [kCGImageSourceShouldCache: false] as CFDictionary
    guard let source = CGImageSourceCreateWithURL(url as CFURL, sourceOptions) else {
        throw ThumbnailError.invalidSource
    }
    let options = [
        kCGImageSourceCreateThumbnailFromImageAlways: true,
        kCGImageSourceCreateThumbnailWithTransform: true,
        kCGImageSourceShouldCacheImmediately: true,
        kCGImageSourceThumbnailMaxPixelSize: maxPixelSize
    ] as CFDictionary
    guard let image = CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex(source, 0, options) else {
        throw ThumbnailError.decodeFailed
    }
    return image
}

at: and maxPixelSize: are external labels. The first guard bounds the requested output's longest dimension. as CFURL and as CFDictionary bridge to Core Foundation API types. Disabling source caching avoids requesting an eager full decoded source cache. Always-create requests thumbnail generation, transform applies orientation metadata, and immediate caching asks for thumbnail decoding now rather than at a later display moment. Index zero deliberately selects the first image.

This example is not a complete hostile-file validator or an aspect-fill crop algorithm. Check input metadata, frame policy, source limits, and output quality for production. A longest-edge bound preserves aspect ratio; an extreme panorama may not fill a square at desired sharpness. Moving its CGImage result across concurrency domains requires the actual SDK's annotations and ownership rules; do not add unchecked Sendable merely to bypass diagnostics.

sections.title: A bounded cache and a released screen are different outcomes
sections.html:
NSCache can evict objects and supports count/cost settings, but do not treat its cost limit as a deterministic hard allocation ceiling or its eviction order as guaranteed LRU. Individual thread-safe cache operations do not make a lookup-plus-compute sequence atomic. Coordinate duplicate work and invalidation through an owning service. A cache key for a transformed image needs source identity or version, requested pixels, crop or transform, and account scope when the resource is private.

The repository's RMImageCache stores files under a caches directory and creates UIImage instances from data or cached paths. RMImageView checks that the returned URL matches its current URL before assigning the image. These are active ownership and stale-image guard examples. They do not demonstrate pixel-size downsampling or a measured memory budget. Avoid declaring a replacement library installed merely because it is familiar from other apps.

Measure route-exit ownership separately from cache retention. A legitimate application-owned public cache may remain after the screen releases; a private account cache needs account and logout rules. Invalidate pending generations so a late request cannot refill cleared state. After repeated route cycles, explain every surviving population and transient peak. Memory specialist work remains necessary for mapped/dirty pages, jetsam diagnostics, unusual formats, and GPU resources when those dominate; the lesson supplies an auditable starting method.

quiz.question: A 300 KB JPEG is displayed in a tiny view. What follows about decoded memory?
options: It must use exactly 300 KB.
It is automatically downsampled to the view's bounds.
Decoded pixels can be much larger; output dimensions and format need their own budget.
quiz.explanation: Compressed bytes and decoded pixels are different representations. View scaling alone does not prove a smaller decode.

quiz.question: Why can a small ArraySlice retain a large amount of storage?
options: It can share and retain the original backing buffer.
It always eagerly deep-copies every element.
Slices disable ARC globally.
quiz.explanation: A slice can keep the larger collection's buffer alive. Copy a genuinely needed small range when the measured lifetime tradeoff warrants it.

quiz.question: A URLSession task starts inside autoreleasepool and completes later. Does that pool cover all callback temporaries?
options: Yes, lexical nesting makes all future work part of the pool.
No, the synchronous pool can drain before the later callback runs.
Only if the callback captures self weakly.
quiz.explanation: Pool lifetime follows synchronous execution. Callback timing and thread context are separate; pools also do not release strongly retained output.

exercise.brief: Use synthetic image files in a scratch Apple-platform target to compare full-size loading with the thumbnail function, and explain a COW/lifetime experiment separately.
steps: Choose image dimensions, orientation, display points/scale, compressed-byte limit, and a requested output pixel bound.
Verify first-frame and aspect/orientation behavior for valid, corrupt, and extreme-aspect sources.
Plan equivalent Allocations/footprint runs with one and several bounded concurrent decodes, then repeated route exits.
Make both arrays observable in a COW mutation example and investigate retaining a small slice of a large fixture.
acceptance: For the thumbnail path, the output longest dimension respects the chosen bound and orientation is correct.
Estimated pixel arithmetic is labeled as estimated, with actual footprint fields left pending until measurement.
Repeated route exits have an ownership explanation for remaining objects and caches.
No pool encloses an await or is claimed to drain future callbacks; invalid source errors remain distinguishable.
exercise.solution:
For an 80-point square at scale three, begin with a 240-pixel output requirement, then account for the desired content mode. A square source can use the 240 longest-edge bound directly. A wide panorama intended to fill the square needs a different decode/crop calculation or an accepted quality policy; do not silently stretch it. The ImageIO function preserves orientation through transform and returns a CGImage. A UIKit display adapter can create the appropriate UIImage with correct scale under the UI's ownership/isolation contract.

Measure compressed bytes, source dimensions, output dimensions, decoded buffer estimate, transient peak, and retained population independently. Run the baseline and thumbnail candidate with the same source and output appearance. Keep fixture creation out of a decode-only interval. The candidate may reduce decoded output storage, but do not claim a peak reduction until the allocation/footprint evidence exists. Multiple overlapping decodes and any retained full-size intermediary can change the conclusion.

For COW, retain both original and edited arrays, mutate the edited element, and verify original remains unchanged. Compare allocation behavior with a uniquely owned mutation under the same optimization settings. Then keep a tiny slice after releasing the original binding and inspect retention; compare with an explicit small Array copy. The worked conclusion separates proven value semantics from implementation-dependent allocation behavior. ARC ownership, temporary autorelease lifetime, and peak pixel storage remain three distinct explanations.
